question: A 7-year-old child has an esotropia measuring 30 prism dioptres in all directions of gaze. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes with a normal fundus. Which single statement BEST describes this strabismus?

answers.text: Incomitant strabismus — the constant angle in all gaze positions indicates neurological muscle weakness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incomitant strabismus CHANGES with gaze direction because one muscle or nerve is specifically weak. A constant (equal) angle in all positions is the hallmark of comitant strabismus.

answers.text: Comitant strabismus — the deviation is equal in all directions of gaze, indicating normal muscle function with a sensorimotor binocular drive failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Comitant (concomitant) strabismus is defined by an equal angle of deviation in all gaze positions, implying the muscles and their nerves are intact. The fault lies in the central binocular fusion/vergence drive. Accommodative esotropia in this age group is the most common cause.

answers.text: Pseudostrabismus — the equal angle rules out a true deviation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pseudostrabismus shows no deviation on cover testing (the corneal reflex is misleading due to a wide nasal bridge). A 30 PD esotropia confirmed on cover test is a genuine deviation.

answers.text: Incomitant strabismus due to medial rectus contracture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Medial rectus contracture (e.g., in thyroid eye disease) would cause the deviation to increase in the direction away from the contracted muscle. The equal angle in all positions argues against this.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key rule: comitant = same angle everywhere (muscles fine, central drive abnormal); incomitant = angle varies with gaze direction (muscle or nerve weak). Always check multiple gaze positions.
Correct. Equal angle = comitant = central binocular drive failure, not a muscle or nerve problem.
